overview: The atlas labels one enormous 1492-1500 polygon “Denendeh (Dënësųłinë́ Nëné)” and classifies it as a state. That title splices different scales: a GNWT teaching resource uses Denendeh for the wider homeland of several regional Dene groups, while Athabasca Denesųłiné communities call their northern Saskatchewan homeland Nuhenéné. The map shape reaches from Lake Athabasca toward Great Slave Lake and northern Manitoba, overlaps other Dene, Cree, Métis, and broad cultural layers, and vanishes in 1500. It is an approximate reconstruction, not a surveyed border or proof of one government. This card therefore centers Dëne Sųłıné / Denesųłiné people while naming evidence by community and date. Community sources describe caribou, fish, water, family responsibilities, elders, children, teaching, land law, language, and living stewardship. Archaeology offers deeper regional histories of herd-following and skilled technology, but an artifact cannot identify its maker without further evidence. Later ethnography and oral history illuminate particular communities under colonial change; they do not freeze daily life in 1492. The endpoint is only an atlas seam. Dëne Sųłıné people, languages, families, and governments continue.

periods.title: The atlas layer opens
periods.summary: The 1492 snapshot introduces a 69-position polygon with an eight-year software interval. Neither the index nor the geometry records a founding assembly, capital, ruler, or surveyed frontier. This first one-year division is an editorial reading aid, and the compound Denendeh-Denesuline label requires identity correction rather than literal state history.

periods.title: Archaeology reaches behind the label
periods.summary: Nothing in the atlas documents a 1493 event. Regional Taltheilei sequences instead trace centuries of camps, herd-following, water crossings, and tool change around the barren-ground caribou ranges. Archaeologists relate Late Taltheilei to ancestral Chipewyan history, but that relationship is an interpretation, not a name written on every excavated object.

periods.title: Families read caribou movement
periods.summary: The year 1494 is not a dated turning point. Łutsël K’é elders describe families watching crossings, animal condition, weather, and reports from hunters, then moving camps as conditions changed. The study records later remembered knowledge, reviewed with the community; it offers a process of learning and adaptation rather than a year-by-year fifteenth-century diary.

periods.title: Plant knowledge varied by person
periods.summary: The atlas supplies no 1495 harvest record. Fieldwork in 1980-1982 with 25 older people in northern Saskatchewan documented uses for at least 72 plant species, while stressing that each person held a smaller repertoire. This later evidence shows specialized and uneven knowledge, not one timeless recipe book or a complete fifteenth-century pharmacy.

periods.title: Learning carries a living language
periods.summary: No source identifies an event in 1496. Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation now supports videos and a community-produced Fort Chipewyan k’aitélé-dialect reader. This modern revitalization work demonstrates living teaching and local variation; it is not a transcript of one Denesųłiné lesson in the atlas year.

periods.title: Land and routes interlock
periods.summary: The 1497 boundary is editorial. Łutsël K’é Dene describe Thaıdene Nëné through ancestors, forest, tundra, water, culture, and responsibilities carried into the future. Such relationships do not become an exclusive border just because an atlas paints one polygon; neighboring peoples, shared places, and the different scale of Nuhenéné remain part of the history.

periods.title: Place names carry knowledge
periods.summary: The 1498 slice marks no sudden naming event. The Thaıdene Nëné relationship plan preserves Dene Yatı place names, pronunciations, and the principle nuwé ch’anıe while warning that languages and dialects vary. It demonstrates living place-based knowledge around Great Slave Lake without making one modern protected-area plan a map of all 1492 Denesųłiné territory.

periods.title: A map seam, not an ending
periods.summary: At 1500 the exact feature disappears, and later snapshots repaint parts of the region with different atlas categories. No community source reports a collective disappearance then. Dënesųłiné testimony and archives continue across later centuries; the changing pixels belong to the atlas, not to a vanished people or an instant handover to another named group.

sections.title: Untangle the atlas name before reading the color

items.text: The imported record combines “Denendeh” with “Dënësųłinë́ Nëné,” calls the result a state, and supplies only a generic Dene summary. Coverage records one approximate feature and no researched card or override. That database bundle is evidence about the atlas’s condition, not evidence for a centralized Denesųłiné kingdom.

Dene Nation says its assemblies rotate among communities across five regions of Denendeh, with people traveling from 30 Dene communities. That broad regional framework is not interchangeable with one people. GNWT’s preferred spelling table gives Dëne Sųłıné for both this particular language and its speakers.

The decoded 1492 geometry is one Polygon with one ring and 69 coordinate positions, spanning roughly 116.77° to 94.31° west and 55.03° to 64.66° north. It contains several Denesųłiné communities, yet also overlays Cree, Métis, Akaitcho, Tłı̨chǫ, and broader atlas layers. Color overlap is not consent or sovereignty.

The exact id occurs in 1492 and nowhere in the audited 1400, 1500, or 1530 snapshots. Several sampled places are blank or receive different labels after the seam. A missing shape can mean a cartographic repaint; it cannot, by itself, mean migration, conquest, extinction, or a new territorial agreement.

Denesųłiné geography is not one uniform block. A Saskatchewan reference distinguishes Athabasca and Churchill River regions and notes differences in resources, adaptations, and speech. It also places Denesuline within a larger Athabascan language family. This card names the community behind each claim instead of converting “Dene” into a universal synonym.

sections.title: Follow homelands, waters, seasons, and routes

items.text: Athabasca Denesųłiné identify Nuhenéné as their homeland and list communities from Lake Athabasca to Wollaston Lake. They say their lives extend beyond provincial and territorial lines because people followed barren-ground caribou. That community account corrects the atlas’s border-like appearance without declaring every route exclusive to one nation.

Nuhenéné is described through land, water, air, plants, animals, rocks, medicines, and spirits. Language is said to describe the land with meanings best understood through that relationship. This is a living Athabasca community account, not a claim that every named feature or teaching can be dated specifically to 1492.

Łutsël K’é community history names Ɂedacho Tué for a major caribou crossing. Families gathered near its southern crossing in fall, then shared, dried, and cached meat. The page also distinguishes earlier canoe-and-spear harvesting, bow-and-arrow cover, twentieth-century cabins, and current travel instead of compressing every practice into 1492.

Northern Saskatchewan Denesuline ranges differ between the Athabasca Basin, where barren-ground caribou arrive more regularly, and the upper Churchill region, where they are less common. Forest cover, marsh, lake, and tundra margins also vary. One polygon therefore hides regional choices rather than defining a single seasonal schedule.

Thaıdene Nëné means “land of the ancestors.” Its relationship plan uses Dene Yatı names for lakes, bays, portages, gathering places, and animal crossings, and says dialects vary within the area. Place names are compact stores of guidance and history, although this modern plan covers one region, not the entire atlas polygon.

sections.title: Build meals from caribou, fish, berries, and plants

items.text: Athabasca Denesųłiné call barren-ground caribou a cultural keystone. Their protocol uses the whole animal: meat nourishes people, hides become clothing and bedding, and bone and antler become crafts. This community teaching demonstrates integrated skill and respect; it does not prove an identical cut, meal, or ceremony in every fifteenth-century camp.

A community land inventory names whitefish, lake trout, pickerel, burbot, jackfish, beaver, moose, caribou, blueberries, Labrador tea, spruce gum, and rat root. It shows the breadth of a living food-and-land relationship. The list is ecological knowledge, not a shopping receipt from 1492 or permission to prescribe medicines.

At Ɂedacho Tué, community history describes families gathering for the fall migration, sharing fresh meat, and drying or caching supplies for winter. Herman Gahdële remembered seeing a crossing as a small child and meat frozen for lean months. The named place and narrator keep the evidence specific rather than universal.

Northern Saskatchewan fieldwork recorded 34 plant species used as foods among 72 useful species discussed by 25 older consultants. Fruit use persisted, while plant foods were seasonal and personal repertoires differed. The study warns against turning a compiled catalogue into the daily menu of every Denesųłiné person.

A Saskatchewan reference describes feasts and tea dances as continuing social practices and notes that caribou availability differs by region. Feasting is more than calorie delivery: it can renew relationships and identity. The modern description cannot supply the exact guest list, recipe, or ritual sequence for an unrecorded gathering in 1492.

sections.title: Make camps, clothing, containers, and precise tools

items.text: Thaıdene Nëné spans the transition between boreal forest and tundra and includes the East Arm of Great Slave Lake, other lakes, and rivers. Łutsël K’é Dene describe this as a living homeland shaped by relationships among people, water, land, forest, and tundra, not an empty backdrop or fixed camp plan.

Museum-linked inventories identify Chipewyan and Late Taltheilei fleshers, bone-splitting wedges, adzes, arrowheads, knives, scrapers, shaft smoothers, antler bow parts, birchbark containers, hide stretchers, awls, needles, and beads. The toolkit shows engineering across stone, bone, antler, wood, bark, hide, and copper, though individual makers remain unnamed.

Taltheilei archaeology documents water-crossing camps, dense stone-working debris, lanceheads, knives, scrapers, and later bow-and-arrow technology across forest and tundra. Researchers connect Late Taltheilei with ancestral Chipewyan history. That is a reasoned archaeological relationship, not proof that each site belonged solely to today’s named Denesųłiné communities.

Caribou hides supplied clothing and bedding, while bone and antler supplied craft material. Archival artifact lists add awls, needles, stretchers, and hide-working tools that made processing possible. The finished coat rarely survives as readily as stone, so a vanished garment can represent many hours of expertise rather than an empty material record.

Rangifer Central reports smaller winter tools than summer examples of the same type and inventories bows, arrows, knives, scrapers, smoothers, containers, and sewing implements. Seasonal differences reveal planning for load, task, and travel, but size alone cannot date a tool, identify its user, or reconstruct an entire household.

sections.title: See families, sharing, leadership, and social life

items.text: A Dene values statement joins shared food and camp work with responsibility for children and family health. It says extended families and communities cared for elders, widows, and orphans. These region-wide principles are direct Dene testimony, but they do not reveal household size, marriage rules, or every Denesųłiné family’s arrangements in 1492.

Łutsël K’é elders described grandfathers, fathers, and sons hunting together, while wives, aunts, mothers, and daughters made garments, bags, fish, and berry packets. Women were also skilled hunters. Families contributed what they could and shared the harvest, making the camp a cooperative network rather than a one-person survival show.

Herman Gahdële remembered being raised on the land by his grandparents and watching caribou cross Ɂedacho Tué when he was three or four. One childhood memory cannot define every family, but it places grandparents, young children, food storage, observation, and place-based learning inside a named community history.

The Dene statement says everyone should be heard and that families, communities, and regions decide matters affecting them. It looks to elders, leaders, and medicine people for guidance rather than service. This does not describe a king, capital, tax office, or chain of command that would justify the atlas’s “state” classification.

Modern Saskatchewan descriptions mention tea dances, hand games, caribou-hide drums, feasts, and regional variation. Such evidence shows social life as celebration, competition, teaching, and relationship together. It cannot date one dance form unchanged to 1492, identify a particular song, or make every Athabasca and Churchill River community’s gathering identical.

sections.title: Let children learn from elders, work, language, and land

items.text: Athabasca Denesųłiné say elders teach young people land survival, raising strong babies, laws, and guiding principles, and contribute at community meetings. Annual culture camps add hunting, drumming, and dancing. The account describes active transmission today and long responsibilities, while avoiding a claim that fifteenth-century learning followed a modern school calendar.

GNWT’s Dene Kede curriculum organizes learning through relationships with the spiritual world, land, self, and people. Its goal is capable citizenship, with meaningful language use woven through experience. This is a five-nation curriculum shaped for schools; it illustrates Dene educational philosophy rather than documenting a 1492 classroom.

The Dene Kede manual was developed with Dene teachers and elders and asks each community to make its own local program. It recommends land experiences, storytelling, elders in classrooms, research, and shared reflection. That local design matters: a generic curriculum is explicitly not a substitute for community-specific knowledge.

At Black Lake, elders join an annual school caribou hunt to teach responsible harvesting. Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation has also produced a Fort Chipewyan-dialect reader with community members and a youth designer. These are modern institutions carrying knowledge forward, not evidence that books or school trips existed in 1492.

The teacher manual says elders’ knowledge and Dene language are central to becoming capable on the land and generous with others. Observation, practice, story, and reflection can work together. Because this source covers several Dene nations, this card treats it as a broad framework and lets named Denesųłiné sources supply local examples.

sections.title: Hear a living language and read one exact sample

items.text: GNWT writes the language and people as Dëne Sųłıné. Its orthography uses a glottal-stop letter, ł, diaeresis, acute marks for high tone, ogoneks for nasalization, and dotless i for clarity. These details matter: deleting marks to make the name easier for software can change a community’s carefully standardized writing.

Written sample: “Ɂedlánetʼe-a?” The GNWT teaching sheet gives the practical pronunciation guide “e-dla-ne-ṯe-a?” and translates it “Hello / How are you?” This is an exact modern Dëne Sųłıné lesson, not a 1492 inscription. No securely dated written Denesųłiné sentence from the atlas interval was identified.

A second official sheet prints “ɂedlánet’e-a” with the guide “ed-lah-neh-teh-ah” for “Hi / Hello,” and “mársı,” pronounced “mar-see,” for “Thank you.” The spelling difference between teaching sheets is worth preserving rather than silently harmonizing; language materials can reflect font, dialect, and editorial choices.

Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation calls its new resource the first reader in the Fort Chipewyan k’aitélé dialect and credits community language workers and a youth designer. That specificity prevents a common mistake: “the Dene language” is not one interchangeable voice, and a local reader should not be relabeled for every Dene nation.

The Thaıdene Nëné plan notes variation within and between languages and dialects and identifies Dene Yatı as one language used in that area. A written sample can welcome readers without flattening that variation. Pronunciation guides are helpful approximations, not replacements for listening to speakers or learning with a community.

sections.title: Respect stories, ceremony, spirituality, and land law

items.text: Łutsël K’é’s community site explains three Dene laws through a protected place, an elders’ map accepted by the community, and a later membership vote. The dates and procedures differ, yet all express ongoing territorial responsibility. This living legal account should not be collapsed into a single timeless rule for the entire atlas polygon.

Łutsël K’é Dene describe caribou as physical, cultural, linguistic, emotional, and spiritual sustenance. Their community-led stewardship plan uses beliefs, values, stories, words, monitoring, education, and respectful-harvest protocols. Those named modern institutions express living law; they do not prove that every protocol had identical wording in 1492.

At Ts’ąkuı Theda, a community-shared creation story joins hunger, failed sharing, prayer, an elder woman’s transformation, healing, respect, and a law to protect the place. It is attributed to Steven Nitah and belongs to Łutsël K’é. Naming source and setting avoids turning one sacred narrative into generic “Dene mythology.”

Athabasca Denesųłiné say the drum begins ceremonies and is treated with respect; elders teach drumming and dancing at annual culture camps. These living practices join performance with teaching and continuity. The source still cannot supply the exact songs, instruments, participants, or choreography of a particular gathering in 1492.

Thanadelthur, a Denesuline woman, served as interpreter and negotiator in 1715-1716, helping establish peace and trade relations. Her achievement belongs to its own eighteenth-century setting, more than two centuries after the atlas seam. Including the date keeps a famous life from being misused as scenery for an undocumented 1492 encounter.

sections.title: Treat medicine, caregiving, and colonial harm with care

items.text: Fieldwork with 25 older Chipewyan consultants recorded medicinal knowledge involving 52 plant species, but the author found small personal repertoires and changing use. This is evidence of specialized northern Saskatchewan knowledge in 1980-1982, not medical advice, a complete formulary, or proof that each remedy was practiced identically five centuries earlier.

Dene principles honor medicine men and women for skills, wisdom, and guidance, while linking good health to law, land, family safety, and care for children and elders. The source names a social role without disclosing treatments. This card therefore describes responsibility and expertise but gives no dose, diagnosis, or do-it-yourself remedy.

In 1960-1962 Snowdrift, fathers were observed carrying small children, comforting them, and helping with infant toilet needs. One four-year-old moved from a household pot with parental help to the outhouse the next summer. It is a warm, specific observation from one later community, not a timeless parenting rule.

Remembering Our Relations places Dënesųłiné oral histories first in documenting eviction from Wood Buffalo National Park, forced family separation, restricted rights, and their effects on health and identity. The harm is twentieth-century colonial history, not the card’s 1500 ending, and community testimony also frames remembrance as part of healing.

Dene Kede asks communities to interpret a broad curriculum locally and places elders, language, land experience, story, and reflection inside learning. That structure argues against “everyone knew every cure.” Expertise could be distributed, learned, and sought from others; no curriculum or card should turn selective knowledge into unsupervised treatment.

sections.title: Manage water and waste, then continue beyond the seam

items.text: Lake Athabasca, Black Lake, Wollaston Lake, waterfalls, rivers, fish, and summer gathering places organize the Athabasca community account. Water is food habitat, route, relation, and responsibility. That importance does not tell us how every 1492 camp selected drinking water, washed utensils, or prevented contamination, so those household details remain open.

VanStone counted twelve outhouses for 26 occupied Snowdrift dwellings in 1961-1962, generally 50 to 75 yards behind houses; some households may have shared, and some people used nearby bushes. The number had risen from four in one year. Even toilets need timestamps: this is settled-village evidence, not 1492 archaeology.

No cited fifteenth-century archaeological source here identifies a Denesųłiné latrine, privy, sewer, or rule for human waste. Camps certainly managed privacy, cleanliness, and refuse, but a pit or midden needs contents and context before it becomes a toilet. The later Snowdrift observations cannot be backdated five centuries to fill that gap.

A Parks Canada historical report traces twentieth-century park rules, harvesting restrictions, displacement, and contested treaty relations in Dënesųłiné homelands. This later rupture belongs in the long history because it changed access and care, yet it cannot be smuggled backward into the atlas’s short 1492-1500 seam.

When the atlas removes the exact id in 1500, it supplies no battle, treaty, epidemic, migration record, or successor polity. Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation’s language work documents living speakers and learners. The honest ending is continuity: a map layer stops rendering, while families, language, lands, and responsibilities do not.

ending.text: The feature ends in 1500 because the atlas stops drawing this exact id. No cited source records a Denesųłiné defeat, evacuation, treaty, epidemic, or political dissolution in that year. The 1530 snapshot assigns some sampled places to other broad layers, while others remain unpainted; neither behavior identifies a historical successor. Dëne Sųłıné people continue across distinct communities, dialects, and governments. Dene Nation assemblies also continue across five regions and 30 Dene communities; that wider Denendeh framework is not a synonym for one people. Later fur trade, epidemics, treaty making, settlement, schooling, parks, mining, and state policy deeply changed lives and access to land, but each belongs to its own documented date. The card therefore closes with continuity rather than a fall. Its one automatic conclusion is about the database: an approximate, overlapping polygon vanished at a software seam. Families, language, law, knowledge, and responsibilities to water, caribou, ancestors, and future generations did not.
